planting.note: Divide offsets in spring and tuck into a shaded, mossy seep wall or crevice with constant trickle moisture; seed germinates slowly and erratically after 60-90 days of cold-moist stratification.

directions: This mat-forming rock-garden alpine carries white, yellow-eyed bell flowers and thrives only where shaded, mossy rock stays constantly wet from seepage or trickle, a niche few flowering perennials can fill. Give it the wettest, shadiest spot available — a seep wall, mossy boulder face, or north-facing crevice — and never let it dry out even briefly, supplementing with hand-misting in cultivation if natural seepage is unreliable. Division of offsets in spring is far more dependable than seed for building up a garden-worthy clump.

planting.note: Plant tuberous offsets or stratified seed in gritty, well-drained soil in a shaded trough or wall crevice; allow a dry summer rest after spring bloom.

directions: A tiny tufted collector's plant from oceanside bluffs of northern California to southern Vancouver Island, this mistmaiden carries white, yellow-throated flowers on a tuberous rootstock built for a drier summer dormancy than its wetter cousin Romanzoffia sitchensis. Plant it in gritty, fast-draining soil in a shaded trough or crevice, and let the soil dry out somewhat after spring bloom rather than keeping it constantly damp. Because its native range is narrow, it is rarely offered commercially, so source from a specialty alpine or native-plant seed supplier rather than expecting to find container stock.

planting.note: Divide rooted rhizome sections in fall and plant into undisturbed, acidic, duff-rich soil under conifers; top-dress with conifer needle litter and never let it dry out.

directions: A naturally occurring, fully fertile hybrid of the familiar eastern bunchberry and its Arctic relative, this Pacific Coast taxon forms a denser, more robust carpet under conifers than Cornus canadensis, with the same white-bracted flower clusters and red berry heads in late summer. It needs the same undisturbed, acidic, humus-rich forest floor as its relative and will not establish in cultivated garden soil without a conifer-litter top-dressing to match. Rhizome division in fall is the reliable propagation route, since seed requires a long combined warm-and-cold stratification and often takes more than a year to germinate.

planting.note: Divide the slender scaly rhizomes in fall and plant into leaf-litter-covered, dappled shade under bigleaf maple or hemlock.

directions: This dainty, trifoliate-leaved woodland anemone carries small white-to-pale-blue-to-pink flowers in spring and works well as a small-scale filler among ferns and trillium where the larger, more common anemones would overwhelm the scene. Plant it among leaf litter in dappled light under deciduous canopy, and expect it to go dormant by midsummer, so pair it with later-emerging ferns to cover the gap it leaves. Division of the rhizomes in fall is far more dependable in cultivation than seed, which germinates slowly and irregularly even after cold stratification.

planting.note: Divide rhizome clumps in spring and plant into moist, humus-rich understory soil in partial to full shade; fills in as groundcover within one to two seasons.

directions: This low, soft-textured native bedstraw gives Pacific Northwest native-plant gardens a straight-species alternative to the European sweet woodruff for knitting together ground under shrubs without becoming aggressive. Plant it in the same moist, humus-rich understory soil sweet woodruff prefers, in partial to full shade. It is pollinated by an unusually broad range of generalist insects, making it a quietly useful insectary groundcover in a restoration-minded planting. Divide and spread clumps in spring to fill bare ground faster.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring, or divide corm clusters in early spring, into humus-rich shaded soil as a textural matrix grass among woodland wildflowers.

directions: A genuinely shade-tolerant bunchgrass with onion-like corms at its base, this species makes a non-aggressive, deer-resistant matrix grass for a woodland native garden rather than a lawn substitute. Plant it among sword fern and trillium rather than in open turf, since it spreads slowly via rhizome and harmonizes with companion wildflowers instead of swamping them. It stays partially evergreen through mild coastal winters and tolerates real drought once established, despite its shaded, moist-forest origins.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring (no stratification needed) or divide tufts into moist, shaded streambank-type soil at the base of vine maple or along a shaded path edge.

directions: Loose, open, drooping panicles on wide, limp leaf blades give this grass an elegant, airy texture under trees, a soft contrast to stiffer ornamental grasses. Give it the moist, shaded streambank conditions it occupies in the wild and let it flop naturally rather than staking it, since the drape is the feature rather than a flaw. It works especially well massed at the base of vine maple or softening a shaded garden path edge.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring or divide clumps into moist-to-dry forest-floor soil under full canopy; this species genuinely thrives in dense shade rather than merely tolerating it.

directions: Unlike the sun-loving ornamental blue fescues common in cultivation, this true forest-floor fescue has soft, hairy leaves and a drooping, narrow inflorescence with distinctively crinkled awns, giving a lawn-type texture to plantings under full canopy where few bunchgrasses perform. Keep soil on the moist-to-dry side rather than waterlogged, since it is adapted to forest-floor drainage, not wetland conditions. Use it as a textural specimen or small drift in deep shade rather than expecting broad turf-like coverage.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Direct sow in spring (no stratification required) onto a shaded, disturbed slope, ravine, or streambank where erosion control and soft texture are both wanted.

directions: This native woodland bunchgrass carries nodding, flattened spikelets on an open, graceful panicle and was traditionally included in Pacific Northwest restoration seed mixes for stabilizing shaded, disturbed slopes. Use it the same way in a garden setting, on a shaded bank or roadcut where erosion control and soft texture are both wanted. It tolerates both moist and fairly dry shaded sites and also performs in more open conditions if the planting isn't purely shade-focused. As a bonus it provides modest wildlife forage value for a restoration-minded planting.
sources: US Forest Service Fire Effects Information System (FEIS)
